title: Trust Recovery
concept: Using the Proof Protocol for a real breach of trust: name what happened, decide what needs to change, set a time window, keep a record of the facts, then check in.
whenToUse: After a betrayal, deception, repeated broken agreements, or any clear before/after change in how safe things feel.
steps: Name what happened, clearly, without deflecting. The partner who broke trust names it and acknowledges the impact; the hurt partner is never asked to confess in return.
Decide on one specific, observable change. Any transparency is offered voluntarily by the partner who broke trust, for a set time — it never becomes monitoring.
Set a real time window, with dates to check in.
Keep a simple table — just the facts — to see and review at the agreed check-in.
Check in — look at the record first, then talk about how it feels. Extend, adjust, or close it out.
If it's not safe, stop and get outside support.

phrases.text: What happened was ___. I'm not debating that.
My proof: ___. You'll see it when ___.

working: Named what happened. Proof: gives a heads-up if running late, plus an open calendar they chose to offer for the window. Checked in weekly for 4 weeks. One partial week, owned honestly. Things feel calmer, so the window gets extended.
notWorking: Long apology speeches with no actual behavior behind them — or pushing for “trust me again” before there's any evidence — or using the record to shame someone. Demanding passwords, tracking location, or reading messages isn't proof; it's monitoring.
activity: Fill in one row of proof and a 4-week table together. Use it alongside the Proof Protocol card.
warn: If it's not safe, stop and get outside support. Transparency is offered by the partner who broke trust, time-limited, and never becomes monitoring — no demanding passwords, location tracking, or reading messages.
note: Deciding not to rebuild, or to end the relationship, is a valid outcome of this protocol, not a failure of it.
